Self-insured plans are a lifeline for businesses crushed by Obama-era overregulation. The Self-Insurance Protection Act (H.R. 2813) slashes bureaucratic red tape, ensuring 103 million Americans keep access to flexible healthcare options without D.C. meddling. Stop-loss insurance isn’t traditional coverage—it’s a financial safeguard letting employers manage risk without surrendering to one-size-fits-all mandates. 

While the previous administration attacked these plans, this bill restores sanity by blocking states from imposing counterproductive rules. Washington’s job isn’t to micromanage healthcare—it’s to enable innovation and choice. This aligns with broader efforts to dismantle burdensome regulations stifling American businesses. 

Let employers lead, not bureaucrats.

The GOP Doctors Caucus pushing CMS to crack down on private insurers’ payment delays post-Change Healthcare cyberattack? About time. The Bipartisan Health Care Act’s Medicaid provisions (Sections 112-113) already expose how middlemen inflate costs through spread pricing and opaque rebate schemes.

If insurers can’t process claims efficiently even after a $1.4B taxpayer-funded bailout of their IT systems, maybe it’s time to audit every dollar flowing through these corporate bureaucracies. Medicare Advantage overpayments hit $83B last year—imagine if that waste funded actual care instead of insurance exec bonuses.

Accountability starts with transparent pass-through pricing, not more Band-Aid fixes for failed systems.

Employer health plans are crucial, but let’s not pretend the status quo works. The Association Health Plans Act (H.R. 2528) cracks open the insurance monopoly by letting small businesses and self-employed workers band together—finally giving them negotiating power against Big Pharma and hospital cartels. Section 3(5)(B) guts the red tape that forces employers into overpriced, one-size-fits-all plans.

KFF data shows family premiums hit $25,572 in 2024 while deductibles soared—proof that D.C.’s regulatory stranglehold drives costs. Real reform isn’t tweaking deductibles; it’s unleashing competition.

Let employers pool risk across state lines, slash administrative bloat, and bypass insurers entirely. Bureaucrats hate this because it exposes their role in propping up a broken system.

Rep. Onder nails it—decades of bloated healthcare policies have crushed competition, leaving Americans trapped in a system rigged for bureaucrats, not patients. The Association Health Plans Act (H.R. 2528) is a rare win for small businesses, letting them pool resources under ERISA to bypass ACA red tape. Section 3(5)(B) guts the "commonality of interest" shackles, allowing realty shops, bakeries, and contractors to band together as large-group buyers.

This isn’t theory: AHPs slash premiums 30% vs. ACA plans by ditching mandates like pediatric dental coverage (Sec. 736(b)(3)) and leveraging bulk pricing. Critics whine about "skinny plans," but when 96% of U.S. firms are small, choice beats centralized collapse.

The 2023 NAIC data shows 85% of new AHPs offered comprehensive care anyway—proving markets self-correct when D.C. steps back.

The numbers and legislative details don’t lie—see the receipts for yourself: https://t.co/plEDQ2trWp

The Self-Insurance Protection Act is a critical step to shield small businesses from state overreach trying to regulate stop-loss coverage into oblivion. H.R. 2571 rightly clarifies that these risk-management tools aren’t health insurance—they’re financial safeguards letting employers self-fund without drowning in unpredictable costs.

The Obama-era obsession with strangling this market (to prop up failing ACA exchanges) shows why federal preemption is necessary: bureaucrats can’t stand anything that bypasses their control. States like New York and California have tried to kill stop-loss by imposing arbitrary attachment points, which would force small businesses into overpriced fully-insured plans.

Your bill blocks that power grab, Rep. Onder. Let’s not pretend this is about “consumer protection”—it’s about preserving D.C.’s ability to funnel employers into broken systems. Real reform means letting markets manage risk, not letting regulators invent new hoops.

Funny thing about “lowering premiums” bills…

Protecting stop loss insurance may help some self insured employers manage catastrophic risk, but it doesn’t automatically lower premiums for families buying coverage, nor does it address the marketplace increases scheduled for January 2026.

Congress has known for years where costs are actually rising  provider consolidation, drug pricing, administrative overhead, and subsidy cliffs. ERISA preemption debates don’t change those fundamentals.

If this bill works, Americans should see measurable reductions not just expanded flexibility for employers already positioned to self insure.

The test isn’t intent or projections.

It’s whether people pay less at renewal.
